newsitem.title: USA: Low inflation brings new challenges to E. Europe.
newsitem.headline: Low inflation brings new challenges to E. Europe.

text.p: Eastern European economies have made big strides in exorcising the demon of inflation but are finding this brings new challenges on the path to growth.

Holes in the budget are harder to fill without sky-high price rises to boost government revenues. Several East European and former Soviet states are finding low inflation is also making life harder for their fledgling banking systems.

"The banking system has come out of the inflation period in a shock and many banks have serious problems with their liquidity," Ukrainian Deputy Prime Minister for the economy Viktor Pynzenyk told a conference on Tuesday during the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank.
"It was very easy to act when zeros were just added to the currency and under these conditions many banks have just eaten up their capital," he added.

Ukraine, helped by an $867 million IMF standby credit, has slashed inflation to about 0.1 percent a month from 182 percent in 1995 and 10,000 percent in 1993. It introduced its hryvnia currency last month, stable at 1.76 to the dollar.
Pynzenyk said final details of a new three-year IMF loan of $2.5-3.0 billion should be finalised this month.
Ukraine is also in talks with the Word Bank over a credit of up to $300 million to restructure the financial sector.
The IMF, in its world economic outlook, says the transition countries, which include Eastern Europe, can look forward to long-term growth of four to five percent a year.
But it says some states' fiscal deficits are too high, tax and wage arrears have built up and more needs to be done to restructure enterprises.

"Without adequate progress in these areas the economic and social costs of the transition will be considerably higher... and the risks of reversal of the economic and political reform process will remain," the IMF said.
Tight monetary policy in Russia has helped cut inflation from 17.8 percent in January 1995 to around 0.3 percent in September. The rouble is in a crawling peg against the dollar.
Russia has made the fight against inflation its key economic goal and it has won the backing of the IMF, which earlier this year agreed a $10 bilion loan deal with Moscow.

But success has caused problems for some Russian banks, which used to rely on sure-fire profits from foreign exchange deals. The economy also has deep payments problems, with many workers not paid for month and companies in huge tax arrears.
Finance Minister Alexander Livshits said on Wednesday that ministers of the Group of Seven rich industrial states had raised the tax issue in talks with the Russian team.
"The general opinion was that the central problem was to bring balance to the budget. If we ensure that, then we will be able to solve all the other problems," he said.
Russia has a $500 million World Bank loan to help cushion the impact of restructuring its coal industry. But budget pressure means Moscow has not used all the first $250 million.
"There is a danger of not receiving the second tranche of that loan," First Deputy Prime Minister Vladimir Potanin said.
Poland, further down the reform road than the Slav giants to the East, saw steep falls in output in the early 1990s.
But Finance Minister Grzegorz Kolodko, in remarks prepared for the IMF/World Bank meeting, said Poland was benefiting from a policy of improving efficiency and competitiveness.
"After the period of shock without therapy the policy of therapy without shock is being exercised," he said.
IMF Managing Director Michel Camdessus on Thursday paid tribute to Poland's achievements, saying it could have West European levels of inflation by the end of the century.
